title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: How Hot Wheels Work
summary: Josh and Chuck present an episode on how Hot Wheels work, part of a Twelve Days of Christmas Toys playlist. They cover the 1968 launch of Hot Wheels by Mattel as a rival to Matchbox, designer Harry Bradley and the first sixteen cars, the Spectra Flame paint and red line tires and working suspension of early models, the move of production from Hawthorne, California to Hong Kong and later Malaysia, the 1970 Saturday morning cartoon Speed Buggy, the 1970 Jack in the Box and 1983 McDonald's Happy Meal releases, the Treasure Hunt series from 1995, the 1996 Mattel purchase of Tyco and Matchbox, branding and licensing deals, scale and wheel design, fantasy cars, die-cast manufacturing, collector values such as the 1968 Beach Bomb, the Python/Cheetah name change, the 2008 diamond-studded fortieth anniversary car, and the 1987 Toledo collector's convention. The episode ends with listener mail about a proposal to tie minimum wage to living costs.
topics: Hot Wheels Python Cheetah name change

segments.title: Opening and playlist introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as part of the Twelve Days of Christmas Toys playlist and says he loved Hot Wheels as a kid. The show's standard opening plays.

segments.title: Banter about childhood toys
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trade stories about their childhood toys, including Josh's missing Hot Wheels collection and Chuck's GI Joe figures, and Josh's book report visual aid.

segments.title: Hot Wheels production numbers and origins
segments.summary: Chuck notes that more than four billion Hot Wheels have been produced since 1968, more than the Detroit big four combined. They discuss the name pronunciation and the 1968 launch in response to Matchbox, with Mattel's Elliott Handler seeing an opening in the die-cast market.

segments.title: First sixteen cars and Harry Bradley
segments.summary: Harry Bradley, a former GM designer, designed the first sixteen Hot Wheels released in 1968, sold for 59 cents each, including the Camaro and a Corvette released before the real 1969 Corvette. Their features included suspension, Red Line tires, and Spectra Flame paint.

segments.title: Performance design versus Matchbox
segments.summary: Hot Wheels were built to race and beat Matchbox cars head to head. Production moved from Hawthorne, California to Hong Kong, and the early features were phased out. Josh notes the axles were designed to reach 200 scale miles per hour.

segments.title: Speed Buggy cartoon and Hot Wheels car designs
segments.summary: Hot Wheels became a Saturday morning cartoon by 1970, the Speed Buggy show. Chuck praises the AMC Pacer and Gremlin variations. Josh contrasts Hot Wheels' performance focus with Matchbox's realism.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Short transition before the next content section.

segments.title: Branded and licensed Hot Wheels
segments.summary: Hot Wheels has many branded and licensed lines, including Ghostbusters, Mars candy vans, Marvel and DC, Fast and Furious, and NASCAR. Hot Wheels have wider wheels to look sporty, and the hosts discuss how scaled-down cars look odd, so the wheel wells are expanded. The Red Baron car's helmet design is discussed.

segments.title: Expansion, Happy Meals, and marketing to children
segments.summary: Hot Wheels had 16, 24, and 33 cars in early releases. In 1970 they appeared at Jack in the Box, and in 1983 they became a McDonald's Happy Meal offering with fourteen cars, including the Chevy Citation and the Toyota Mini Trek camper. The hosts discuss marketing to children and an Australian ban.

segments.title: Treasure Hunt series and the Oldsmobile 442
segments.summary: In 1995 Mattel released the Treasure Hunt series, a limited run of twelve models at around 10,000 each, which later became common. The hosts discuss the Oldsmobile 442 and a friend's muscle car.

segments.title: Mattel acquires Tyco and Matchbox
segments.summary: In 1996 Mattel bought Tyco, which made Matchbox, so Hot Wheels and Matchbox became owned by the same company.

segments.title: Design process, scale modeling, and fantasy cars
segments.summary: Early designers measured real cars with tape measures; designers like Harry Bradley, Howard Reese, and Larry Wood are legendary. Hot Wheels has fantasy cars that do not exist in real life, unlike Matchbox. Josh mentions a museum exhibit of full-size Hot Wheels cars at the Peterson Automotive Museum.

segments.title: Die-casting and manufacturing today
segments.summary: Modern designs use computer design and 3D printing for prototypes, then molds are made and molten metal is injected under pressure in die-casting. Mainline cars still cost about a dollar.

segments.title: Valuable and rare Hot Wheels
segments.summary: The 1968 Beach Bomb is among the most valuable regular Hot Wheels; a pink version sold for about $75,000 in 2000 and about $125,000 in 2011. The Python was originally called Cheetah until GM's lawyers objected, so some carry the Cheetah name on the base. The Star Wars recall comparison is discussed.

segments.title: Knockoff toys gallery and diamond fortieth anniversary car
segments.summary: Chuck recommends a website gallery of knockoff toys. Josh describes a 2008 fortieth anniversary Hot Wheels car with about 2,700 diamonds and rubies, costing about $140,000 to make.

segments.title: Mad Max, Vanishing Point, and off-topic talk
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the diamond car's resemblance to Mad Max's car, a Mad Max reboot, the film Vanishing Point, and a James Taylor trip to France.

segments.title: First Hot Wheels convention in Toledo
segments.summary: Chuck says the first Hot Wheels collectors convention was held in 1987 in his hometown of Toledo, Ohio, and promotes the HowStuffWorks search bar.

segments.title: Listener mail on minimum wage
segments.summary: Josh reads listener mail from Joe Prohaska in Reno, Nevada, proposing that minimum wage be set based on what a family needs or as a low entry-level starting wage. The hosts discuss cost of living and invite listener responses.

segments.title: Sign-off and sponsor read
segments.summary: Chuck gives contact information and the show closes. Josh then reads a brief sponsor message about Jeff Bridges' Dreaming with Jeff project, sponsored by Squarespace.
